hiragana.title: Letters Practice
hiragana.subtitle: Learn the ICAO code word for every letter with fast, focused drills.

what.title: What is the NATO phonetic alphabet?
what.body: The NATO phonetic alphabet assigns a code word to every letter, from Alfa for A to Zulu for Z. It lets people spell words clearly over radio or phone when letters sound alike.

how.title: How to practice letters effectively
bullets: Practice in short sessions daily (5 to 15 minutes).
Mix recognition with typing drills.
Review missed letters immediately and repeat weak pairs.
Use Blitz once your accuracy is stable.

katakana.title: Codes Practice
katakana.subtitle: Learn radio phrases and digit code words with clear feedback and steady progress.

what.title: What are radio codes?
what.body: Radio codes are short, agreed phrases used in voice communication. They keep messages brief and unambiguous, whether you are saying Zero, Niner, Roger or Mayday.

how.title: How to practice radio codes effectively
bullets: Focus on the phrases you confuse most often.
Practice recognition and typing, not just reading.
Review mistakes until the meaning is automatic.
Work through all five tiers over time.

bullets: Interactive drills across five tiers.
Progress tracking that targets what you miss.
Blitz mode to build speed.
Gauntlet mode for full coverage.

kanji.title: Spelling Practice
kanji.subtitle: Spell words with ICAO code words using fast drills and progress tracking.

what.title: What is callsign spelling?
what.body: Callsign spelling uses code words for each letter of a word. Saying Sierra Oscar Sierra is clearer than spelling S-O-S letter by letter, especially over a noisy radio link.

how.title: How to practice spelling effectively
bullets: Learn the A to Z code words first.
Start with short words before callsign length strings.
Review missed words often.
Use timed drills once the code words are familiar.
